summary: A stopped server now says it is stopped instead of claiming its host is offline
Restart and shutdown notices reach players within seconds instead of after the shutdown had already finished
A session whose byte stream lost data is refused instead of resumed, so an edge restart ends in a clean disconnect rather than a protocol error
Shutdown logs whether a sibling edge exists to take the players over; with none, open sessions will drop and the log now says so
On restart the edge now says whether the splice can actually move players to a sibling, and names why a sibling was unusable
The splice sidecar no longer reports itself as permanently unhealthy; it was answering the edge's health probe, which it never serves

Players are no longer disconnected when the edge they are routed through restarts; the player-to-server direction is now resent after a failover instead of being lost. Takes effect once the pinned splice image is moved to the current splice tag
The node now tracks how much player data the Minecraft server actually received, so an edge failover can resume the connection exactly where it left off

An edge restart no longer disconnects players immediately: if the first edge the session moves to cannot complete the handover, the splice now tries the next one and falls back to the previous behaviour instead of ending the session

An edge restart no longer ends in a connection reset: a failed handover now disconnects cleanly and the player reconnects, instead of resuming the session with missing data that the Minecraft server rejects
Edge restarts no longer disconnect players: the handover was miscounting the connection handshake, so it rejected every resume as damaged even when nothing was lost
Edge logs stay readable during a failover on a busy server: per-player lines are now grouped into one line per event with a count, instead of one line per player
After an edge goes down the splice no longer moves players back to it too early, which caused a second unnecessary handover per restart

The tunnel agent now offers Core and Redis on two local ports and keeps the real addresses up to date itself, so a machine on your hardware survives a platform address change with a few retries instead of a manual edit
Tunnel agent status lines (applied commands, rejected settings, bad input) now appear in the container log instead of only in a place nothing reads
An unreachable platform address no longer makes the tunnel agent ask the platform for a new one back to back; it now waits between attempts

An edge failover can no longer hand a player a stream with a gap in it: one of the two paths that buffer server output during the handover dropped data silently when it filled up, so the session was resumed as if nothing was lost and the Minecraft client failed with a packet error instead of reconnecting

A server stopped because its storage quota is full now tells players exactly that, instead of reporting the host as offline; the host was never the problem and the message pointed everyone at the wrong thing

A route whose target port fell outside 1-65535 was accepted and stored, then silently ignored by every edge, so the domain was simply dead with nothing logged; such a route is now rejected and the reason recorded.

A queued routing change the hub could not process without crashing brought the hub down and was put back at the front of the queue on restart, so it crashed again on every start with no way out; such a message is now dropped with the reason recorded instead.
Updated the Postgres driver, which carried a memory-safety bug and mishandled dollar-quoted strings in a way that could change how a query was parsed.
The route-only link's status endpoint now really binds to loopback. It was given a host:port value that the code turned into an invalid address, so the endpoint silently never started.
The tunnel interface is now named dylaris-wg0 instead of wg0, so it can no longer take over a WireGuard interface you already run. If you pinned WG_INTERFACE to wg0, change it to dylaris-wg0.

A machine whose overlay address is reassigned - which happens when a suspension is lifted - now picks the new address up within half a minute. It used to keep the old one, so the tunnel handshaked and reported healthy on both ends while nothing got through, until the ten-minute re-enrol repaired it.
Upgrading past the interface rename now removes the old wg0 tunnel it left behind, but only when its key proves it was ours. A WireGuard interface you set up yourself is never touched.

The hub admin UI can now create and delete routes, not just list them. Pick the link a route should reach from a dropdown of your links by name, give it a domain and a target address. This is what lets a gateway be run on its own, without a panel in front of it.

Links can now be created and deleted in the hub admin UI. Name a link, copy its token onto the machine that runs it, then point routes at it by that name. Deleting a link that routes still use is refused and tells you how many.

A link can now carry its own display name via the LINK_NAME setting, so the hub shows "Home PC" instead of a node id. Renaming the link in the hub still wins: the name a person picked is never overwritten by the link reporting in.

The hub can now run the warp overlay on its own, so external machines can join a gateway that has no panel behind it. Add a region in the admin UI, create an enrolment key per machine, and it appears with the overlay address it was given. Removing it there drops its tunnel.

A machine now warns at startup when the subnets it routes over the tunnel include the address of the leader it dials. That mistake builds a tunnel that sends everything and receives nothing, with no error to go on.

Creating a link now shows the ready-to-run compose file with the key already in it, and every link has a Deploy button that shows it again later with a placeholder where the key goes. Rolling a key retires the old one and shows the new file straight away.

A machine on someone else's hardware now needs only ONE secret for both of its containers, and never the cluster secret. The hub hands out the tunnel token and database credentials itself at every boot.

A machine that stops warp no longer keeps its WireGuard interface and routes behind. Until now those survived the container and quietly sent the tunnelled networks into a dead device, with nothing left on the machine to point at the cause.

A warp region created in the admin UI now actually reaches the leader. The leader refuses to start without a subnet for its region and had no way to learn one, so a standalone gateway could only be started by repeating the same number by hand in its compose file.

The leader's public key is now worked out for you when adding a region. It could only be read off a leader that was already running, and the leader could not run until the region existed; a wrong value built tunnels that never connected and said nothing.
The single-host compose file now switches the admin UI and the control-plane API on. Started as shipped it gave you a hub with no way in at all.

The hub now refuses to hand an enrolling machine a database address that machine cannot use, such as a Docker service name, and says so on the deploy page. That address arrives as a link which simply never connects.
Rolling a machine's key no longer costs it its overlay address. Each roll used to leave a second entry and an unreachable tunnel behind, slowly using up the region's addresses.

Links that run inside your own stack no longer offer a deploy kit or a key to roll. They authenticate with the cluster secret, so the kit asked for a key that never existed and rolling reported success while changing nothing.
The confirmation shown before rolling a key now describes what happens: the old key stops being accepted at once, but the machine keeps running until its next restart.

Services that fetch their database credentials at startup no longer crash-loop on a cold start. Before the hub's name resolves, the request can reach an unrelated host through wildcard DNS, and its reply was taken as a rejection from us; it is now retried, and a reply that did not come from the hub is refused instead of being used.

The links table no longer shows a Tunnels count. It was summed from a value nothing has ever written, so it read 0 on every link however busy it was - which says 'nobody is connected' rather than 'not measured'.

Deleting a link, or removing a machine on the Warp page, now retires its enrolment key. Until now the key kept working: a removed machine re-joined the overlay by itself within minutes on a fresh address, and a deleted customer's key still returned a working tunnel.
The API now refuses to delete a link that routes still point at, the way the admin UI already did. Deleting through the API left those routes aimed at a link that no longer exists.
The hub now manages DNS itself: a new DNS page holds the provider credential and the zones it may write into, and it keeps the edge wildcards and the beam relay address pointed at whatever is online

The hub can now obtain the beam relay's TLS certificate for you. Turn it on under Certificates on the DNS page: it uses the same provider token over the DNS-01 challenge, renews on its own, and hands the certificate to each relay. A certificate you mount yourself still wins.
The DNS provider credential can now be entered from the platform panel instead of the hub's own interface. The hub still stores it and still owns the records; the panel just forwards the form.

Certificates can now be switched on from the platform panel as well, not only from the hub's own DNS page. That page needs the hub's admin interface, which is off by default, so a deployment running the platform alongside the gateway previously had no way to reach the switch at all.
A DNS credential can now be tested before it is saved, and the test lists the zones the token can actually see.
Testing a DNS credential without retyping the token now only works for the provider that token belongs to, instead of sending it to whichever provider was named.
Saving DNS or certificate settings while a renewal was running could freeze certificate handling until the gateway was restarted.
Switching the DNS provider without entering that provider's token is now refused, instead of quietly reusing the previous provider's token.
A DNS record the gateway could not update no longer gets deleted after the grace period; only names that are genuinely no longer in use are removed.
Removing a customer link on the platform's instruction now removes its routes too; they used to stay live and keep serving traffic for a customer who was gone.
Gateway services no longer send their signed hub credential request to whatever answers when the hub name has not resolved yet, which could hand a working token to an unrelated host.
